title: How to Make a Landing Page Load Faster
content:
A landing page can look simple and still feel slow. A large hero image may delay the main message, a late font may move the call to action, and third-party scripts may compete with the browser before visitors can interact. Improving speed starts by identifying the page's real bottleneck, then changing one cause at a time. A smaller download is useful only when it improves the experience people actually receive.

Establish a reproducible starting point

Record the page URL, device class, connection profile, browser, and build revision. Test a production-like build with the same consent state a visitor sees. A development server can hide or introduce delays that do not represent the deployed page. Use browser developer tools to inspect the network waterfall and the element identified as Largest Contentful Paint, or LCP. Run more than one load because caching and network variation can change the result.

Lab data helps locate a problem; field data describes what actual visits experienced under their own conditions. Neither should be reduced to one unqualified score. If the page serves different hero variants or languages, inspect a representative sample. A fast warm cache can coexist with a poor first visit. Keep a short record of the initial measurements and the element involved so the next experiment can be compared fairly.

Google's LCP optimization guide divides the metric into time to first byte, resource load delay, resource load duration, and element render delay. That breakdown is useful for choosing whether to work on the server, discovery of the image, transfer size, or rendering.

Make the main content discoverable early

Inspect the LCP element before changing every asset. If it is the hero image, use an actual image element where practical, include responsive candidates and a sizes declaration that reflects layout width, and serve an appropriately compressed format. Avoid a huge source that is displayed at a fraction of its dimensions. If the hero is essential on initial view, do not mark it for lazy loading. Check that the browser discovers the image early in the document rather than waiting for JavaScript to render it.

If a background image is necessary for the design, assess whether preload improves discovery without creating competing high-priority downloads. A preload is a claim about criticality; overusing it can delay more important resources. For text-heavy landing pages, the LCP element may be a heading rather than an image. In that case, server response, CSS, web fonts, and rendering delays may matter more than image compression.

Minimize work before the first meaningful paint. Remove unused blocking styles, defer scripts that are not needed to render the opening view, and reserve the analytics and chat widgets for the point at which their functions are required. Check consent and accessibility behavior after moving a script. A page that paints quickly but loses a working form is not improved. Server caching and content delivery can reduce response time, but first measure where time is spent.

Prevent visual jumps

Assign image dimensions or an aspect ratio so layout space exists before media arrives. Reserve space for embeds, consent banners, and dynamic offers. A font swap can change line breaks and push a button downward; inspect font loading and fallback metrics when a shift appears near the headline. Do not solve a shift by hiding meaningful content until an arbitrary timer expires. That changes the problem rather than addressing its cause.

Google's CLS guide describes common layout-shift causes, including images without dimensions, dynamically injected content, and web fonts. The metric is about unexpected movement, so inspect a recording of the shift rather than assuming the largest file is responsible.

Work through one hypothesis at a time

Suppose a hypothetical event landing page displays a 2400-pixel photograph in a 900-pixel region, then inserts a signup strip above the headline after load. The team makes two separate changes. First, it generates responsive image variants and checks the network request chosen at a narrow viewport. Second, it reserves the strip's space before rendering. The first change targets download and discovery; the second targets movement. They test each revision under the original profile and verify that the image remains sharp enough for its purpose.

This is a hypothetical diagnostic sequence, not a measured speed claim. If the LCP element turns out to be text, the image change may barely affect LCP. If the strip appears only after a user action, it may have a different impact than an automatic insertion. The correct next step depends on observed timing and behavior, not on a generic performance recipe.

Use a release checklist that includes function

Before release, confirm the hero's source and rendered dimensions, responsive image selection, and whether critical content is present in the initial HTML. Check the network waterfall for unnecessary early requests and inspect any long task that blocks interaction. Confirm that images and embeds reserve space. Test with fonts available and with delayed font loading. Verify the primary button and form by keyboard, including error states, after any script changes.

Then test narrow and wide viewports, a cold load and a return load, and any important consent state. Note which version and environment produced each observation. Compare the same metric distribution where field data is available; do not report a single favorable laboratory run as a universal visitor result. Revert a change if it worsens critical behavior even when a score rises. Speed work is successful only to the extent that it makes the intended page easier to see and use under the conditions being measured.

Know when to stop optimizing

Every extra technique has a maintenance cost. A complex preload strategy or image pipeline may be reasonable for a frequently visited page with a measured bottleneck, but excessive for a low-traffic experiment without reliable instrumentation. Prioritize obvious waste, broken layout, and delayed essential content first. Document the remaining bottleneck and its estimated cause. Future editors can then add images or scripts without silently undoing the improvement.
